0.title: The Law of Love for the People of Grace
0.essay:
The Ten Commandments are among the most famous words ever spoken. For centuries they shaped the laws and morals of nations. Children memorised them, and churches painted them on their walls. Today many people know little about them, and many Christians are unsure how they apply.

Questions

Are they still binding? Were they only for Israel? Does grace make the law irrelevant? The Bible’s answer is rich.

Grace first

The commandments begin not with a demand but with a reminder of grace: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (Exodus 20:2). God rescued his people first, then gave them his law. The law was never a ladder to climb up to God. It was a way of life for those he had already redeemed.

Love spelled out

Jesus summed up the law in two great commandments: love God with all your heart, and love your neighbour as yourself (Matthew 22:37–39). The Ten fall into those two tables: the first four about love for God, the last six about love for neighbour. And Jesus showed that each reaches the heart, not only outward behaviour.

The chapters

The Law and the Christian; No Other Gods, No Images; God’s Name and God’s Day; Honour and Life; Faithfulness and Property; and Truth, Contentment and the Law Fulfilled.

1.title: The Law and the Christian
1.essay:
God spoke the Ten Commandments to Israel at Sinai after he had rescued them from Egypt. The order is crucial. Obedience is not the way to become God’s people; it is the response of those who already are.

Grace before law

Before a single command, God identifies himself: “the LORD your God”, the rescuer (Exodus 20:2). The commandments are spoken to a redeemed people, and every one should be read in that light. God is not a tyrant laying down rules for slaves. He is a Saviour describing life in freedom.

The same is true for Christians. We are saved by grace through faith, not by keeping the law (Ephesians 2:8–9). But saved people are called to live God’s way.

The law is good

“So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good” (Romans 7:12). It reflects God’s own character. It is not arbitrary; it describes what love looks like. “Oh how I love your law! It is my meditation all the day” (Psalm 119:97).

The law shows our sin

“For by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight, since through the law comes knowledge of sin” (Romans 3:20). The law is like a mirror: it shows our true condition and drives us to Christ. Paul says he would not have known what coveting was if the law had not said, “You shall not covet” (Romans 7:7). The commandment exposed the covetousness in his heart, and sin used it to bring death. The problem is not the law, but us.

When the rich young ruler asked what he must do to inherit eternal life, Jesus listed several commandments. The man said he had kept them all since his youth. Then Jesus, “looking at him, loved him”, and told him to sell all he had and follow him (Mark 10:21). The man went away sorrowful. The law had exposed the idol he loved more than God.

Christ fulfils the law

“Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them” (Matthew 5:17). He kept the law perfectly in our place. “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). And he fulfils it in us by his Spirit, writing it on our hearts (Jeremiah 31:33; Romans 8:4).

Then Jesus said something shocking: “unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:20). Theirs was outward. He calls for a righteousness of the heart, which only he can give.

Jesus deepens the law

In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus shows that the commandments reach the heart. Anger is the root of murder. Lust is adultery in the heart. The law is not satisfied with outward conformity; it calls for a pure heart, which only the Spirit can give. When a lawyer asked which commandment was greatest, Jesus answered with two — love God and love your neighbour — and said, “On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets” (Matthew 22:40). The Ten Commandments are love spelled out.

Three uses of the law

The Reformed tradition speaks of three uses. First, the law restrains evil in society. Second, it shows sinners their need and drives them to Christ. Third, it guides believers in grateful living. Christians are not under the law as a way of salvation, but they delight in it as a guide.

Moral, ceremonial and civil

The law of Moses included moral laws, summed up in the Ten Commandments; ceremonial laws — sacrifices, food laws and festivals; and civil laws for Israel as a nation. The ceremonial laws were “a shadow of the good things to come” (Hebrews 10:1) and are fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17). The civil laws expired with Israel as a nation, though their justice still instructs. The moral law reflects God’s unchanging character and continues to guide Christians.

Two errors

Legalism tries to earn God’s favour by keeping rules, or adds human rules to God’s law. Lawlessness, sometimes called antinomianism, says grace means the law no longer matters. Scripture rejects both. Grace saves us and then teaches us to obey: “the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions” (Titus 2:11–12).

A new Christian assumes the Ten Commandments belong to the Old Testament and have nothing to do with her. Studying them, she discovers that they describe the life Jesus lived and the life the Spirit is producing in her. She begins to read them as a portrait of love, not a list of restrictions.

Do you see God’s law as a burden, a ladder or a guide? Psalm 119 sees it as a delight.

For reflection

Why does it matter that the commandments begin with God’s rescue from Egypt? Which of the three uses of the law do you most need? How does Jesus deepen the commandments in the Sermon on the Mount? Do you lean more toward legalism or lawlessness, and how does the gospel correct you?

2.title: No Other Gods, No Images
2.essay:
“You shall have no other gods before me” (Exodus 20:3). The first commandment is first because everything depends on it. God alone is to be worshipped, trusted, loved and obeyed.

One God

Israel was surrounded by nations with many gods. God’s people were to have one. Their great confession, the Shema, declared it: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one. You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might” (Deuteronomy 6:4–5). These words were to be on the heart, taught to children, spoken at home and on the road, and written on doorposts. Love for God was to shape all of life.

The first commandment does not allow divided loyalty. On Mount Carmel Elijah challenged Israel: “How long will you go limping between two different opinions? If the LORD is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him” (1 Kings 18:21). Israel wanted both.

Modern idols

Few people today bow to statues, but idolatry is everywhere. An idol is anything we trust, love or fear more than God: money, career, comfort, reputation, relationships, pleasure, even family. Paul calls covetousness idolatry (Colossians 3:5). The question is not whether we worship, but what.

John ends his first letter by declaring that the Son of God has come and given us understanding to know the true God: “He is the true God and eternal life.” And then: “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (1 John 5:20–21). Knowing the true God is the best protection against false ones.

A Christian man realises that his anxiety about money shows that he trusts his savings more than God. He has never bowed to a statue, but money has become his working god. He confesses it as idolatry, begins giving generously and learns to trust God for the future.

No images

“You shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth. You shall not bow down to them or serve them” (Exodus 20:4–5). The first commandment governs whom we worship; the second governs how. God may not be represented by images, because no image can capture him. “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:24).

While Moses was on the mountain, the people demanded gods to go before them. Aaron made a golden calf, presented it as the god who brought them out of Egypt, and proclaimed, “Tomorrow shall be a feast to the LORD” (Exodus 32:5). They thought they were worshipping the true God through an image. God called it idolatry. Within weeks of hearing them, they had broken the first two commandments. Images reduce God to something we can see, control and shape to our own ideas.

A jealous God

God attaches a warning and a promise: “for I the LORD your God am a jealous God … but showing steadfast love to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments” (Exodus 20:5–6). His jealousy is not petty but protective, the right jealousy of a husband for his wife. He will not share his glory with idols that destroy his people. And his covenant love reaches to thousands, far beyond his judgment.

Worshipping God his way

The second commandment underlies the Reformed regulative principle: God must be worshipped as he has commanded, not according to human invention. The Worship and the Lord’s Day study explores this.

Pictures of Jesus?

Some Reformed Christians hold that the second commandment forbids any picture of Christ, since he is God and no image can represent his divine nature. Others hold that because the Son became a visible man, depicting his humanity for teaching is permissible, provided images are never used in worship.

Images must never be used as aids to worship, prayed to or venerated. Beyond that, Christians should be very cautious. Any picture of Jesus is imagined, and it can shape and limit how we think of him. Scripture gives no description of his appearance, perhaps deliberately. We know him through the word.

What do you think about most, fear losing most, and turn to for comfort? That may be your idol.

For reflection

What are the most common idols in your culture, and in your own heart? Why does God forbid images in worship? Read Exodus 32: how did Israel break the first two commandments while thinking they were worshipping God? What would it mean to love God with all your heart, soul and might this week?

3.title: God’s Name and God’s Day
3.essay:
The third and fourth commandments protect God’s name and God’s time. Both call for reverence and trust.

The third commandment

“You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not hold him guiltless who takes his name in vain” (Exodus 20:7). God’s name stands for his character and reputation. To take it in vain is to treat it as empty or worthless.

In Israel it was so sacred that misusing it was a capital offence. When a man in a fight “blasphemed the Name, and cursed”, he was brought to Moses, and God commanded that he be put to death (Leviticus 24:10–16).

Ways we misuse it

The most obvious is using God’s name as a swear word or casual exclamation. But the commandment goes further. It is broken by false oaths made in God’s name, by claiming God’s authority for our own ideas (“God told me…”), by careless or irreverent talk about God, and by hypocrisy, when people who bear his name live in ways that dishonour him. Paul told his readers that because of them, “the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles” (Romans 2:24).

A young man has always used “Oh my God” as a casual exclamation without thinking. After studying the third commandment he notices it, and decides to stop. He finds that his reverence for God grows as he guards his speech about God.

Hallowed be your name

The positive side of this commandment is the first petition of the Lord’s Prayer: “Hallowed be your name” (Matthew 6:9). The prayer begins not with our needs but with God’s name, kingdom and will. We ask God to make his name honoured, in our lives and in the world. We are to speak of him with reverence, praise his name and live so that others honour it.

Oaths

Jesus said, “Do not take an oath at all … Let what you say be simply ‘Yes’ or ‘No’” (Matthew 5:34, 37). Most Christians have understood this as forbidding casual or manipulative oaths rather than solemn oaths in court, since God himself, “since he had no one greater by whom to swear, … swore by himself” (Hebrews 6:13).

The fourth commandment

“Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days you shall labor, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God” (Exodus 20:8–10). Rest extended to everyone in the household, including servants, foreigners and animals. The Sabbath was rooted in creation, as God rested on the seventh day, and in redemption, as Israel was freed from slavery (Deuteronomy 5:15). It was a weekly reminder that life depends on God, not on our labour.

Fulfilled in Christ

When the Pharisees criticised his disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath, Jesus said, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27–28). The one who made the Sabbath has authority over it. And he offers the rest it pictured: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). Paul calls the Sabbath a shadow, of which Christ is the substance (Colossians 2:16–17). “So then, there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9), entered by ceasing from our own works and trusting Christ, and completed in glory.

How does it apply?

Many Reformed Christians hold that the fourth commandment remains a moral law, with Sunday as the Christian Sabbath, kept by rest from ordinary work and recreation. Others hold that the Sabbath was part of Israel’s covenant sign — “a sign between me and you throughout your generations” (Exodus 31:13) — fulfilled in Christ.

The Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, as Colossians 2:16–17 and Romans 14:5–6 show. Yet the principle of rest and the gathering of the church on the Lord’s Day remain. The early church met on the first day, the day of resurrection (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10), and that is a clear apostolic pattern. The rhythm of rest God built into creation remains wise and good. We are not machines, and regular rest is an act of trust. Christians who differ on this should not judge one another (Romans 14:4–6). The Worship and the Lord’s Day study treats it more fully.

Do you speak of God casually or reverently? Do you ever claim his authority for your own opinions?

For reflection

In what ways besides swearing can God’s name be “taken in vain”? How can you hallow God’s name in daily life? How is the Sabbath fulfilled in Christ? How could you use the Lord’s Day for worship and rest?

4.title: Honour and Life
4.essay:
The second table of the law begins with the family, and with life itself.

Honour your parents

“Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you” (Exodus 20:12). Paul notes that it is “the first commandment with a promise” (Ephesians 6:2). Honour includes obedience for children — “Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right” (Ephesians 6:1) — respect at every age, and care for parents in old age. And honour flows both ways: “Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord” (Ephesians 6:4).

The Pharisees had a tradition that let people declare their money “Corban”, given to God, and so avoid supporting their parents. Jesus condemned it as “making void the word of God by your tradition” (Mark 7:13). Religion can never be an excuse for neglecting family duty.

Ruth honoured her mother-in-law Naomi by staying with her and providing for her. And Jesus, dying on the cross, made sure his mother would be cared for: “Woman, behold, your son!” he said, entrusting her to John (John 19:26–27). Even in agony, he kept the fifth commandment.

Wider authority

The fifth commandment also shapes how we relate to the other authorities God has set in place: government, employers, church leaders. Honour does not mean blind obedience. When human commands conflict with God’s, “we must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). But it means respect and appropriate submission.

When parents fail

Some parents are abusive, absent or ungodly. Honouring them does not mean pretending, obeying sinful commands or exposing ourselves to harm. It may mean speaking respectfully, praying for them, forgiving them and caring for their needs as far as is wise.

A woman whose elderly father was harsh and critical throughout her childhood struggles to know how to honour him. With counsel, she decides to visit regularly, care for his practical needs and speak respectfully, while not exposing herself to his verbal abuse. She has forgiven him, though trust has not been fully restored.

You shall not murder

“You shall not murder” (Exodus 20:13). Human life is sacred because people are made in God’s image: “Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image” (Genesis 9:6). After the flood, God established that whoever takes a human life will be held accountable. Every human life bears his image.

The commandment forbids murder, the unjust taking of human life, including abortion, euthanasia and suicide. Scripture permits the state to execute justice (Romans 13:4) and recognises self-defence (Exodus 22:2). Christians have differed over war, capital punishment and pacifism, but all agree that innocent life must be protected.

Scripture treats unborn children as persons known by God (Psalm 139:13–16; Jeremiah 1:5; Luke 1:41–44). Abortion takes innocent human life. Yet those who have been involved in abortion can find full forgiveness in Christ.

Murder in the heart

“You have heard that it was said to those of old, ‘You shall not murder; and whoever murders will be liable to judgment.’ But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matthew 5:21–22). Murder begins in the heart, in anger, insults and contempt. “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15).

And Jesus gives urgent instructions at once: “So if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go. First be reconciled to your brother” (Matthew 5:23–24). Settle with your accuser quickly. Anger must be dealt with before it grows. Dealing with it is part of keeping this commandment.

The positive command

The sixth commandment calls us to protect and preserve life: caring for the sick, defending the vulnerable, making peace and looking after our own health.

Is there anger in your heart toward someone that Jesus would call a form of murder?

For reflection

How can you honour your parents, whatever your age or their character? Why does Jesus connect anger and contempt with murder? How does the image of God shape your view of human life? Is there someone you need to be reconciled with this week?

5.title: Faithfulness and Property
5.essay:
The seventh and eighth commandments both concern faithfulness: to our spouse and to what belongs to others. Both protect relationships of trust.

You shall not commit adultery

“You shall not commit adultery” (Exodus 20:14). Marriage is a covenant between one man and one woman for life, and sexual union belongs within it. Adultery betrays a spouse, breaks a covenant and harms children and families.

Jesus takes the commandment to the heart: “But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28). Then he calls for radical action: cut off whatever causes you to sin. The commandment covers lust, pornography and all sexual immorality, in thought, word and deed. It is kept not only by avoiding the act but by guarding the eyes and the heart. And it calls for positive faithfulness: cherishing one’s spouse.

Proverbs warns that adultery is like carrying fire: “Can a man carry fire next to his chest and his clothes not be burned?” (Proverbs 6:27). A thief who steals when he is hungry may be pitied, though he must repay. But the adulterer “destroys himself”, and his disgrace will not be wiped away (Proverbs 6:32–33).

Yet there is hope for the guilty. David committed adultery and was forgiven when he repented (Psalm 51). Jesus forgave sexual sinners and called them to new life. No sexual sin is beyond the reach of grace. The Biblical Sexuality study treats this commandment more fully.

You shall not steal

“You shall not steal” (Exodus 20:15). Stealing is taking what belongs to another. It includes obvious theft, but also fraud, cheating on taxes, wasting an employer’s time, failing to pay debts, plagiarism, and exploiting workers with unjust wages: “Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, are crying out against you” (James 5:4).

During the conquest of Jericho, Achan stole silver, gold and a cloak devoted to God and hid them in his tent. His sin brought defeat on all Israel (Joshua 7). Hidden theft has public consequences.

A Christian employee realises she has been spending an hour a day on personal browsing at work. She sees it as stealing from her employer, confesses it to God, changes her habits and works with new diligence. Her manager notices, and later promotes her.

From taker to giver

Paul gives the alternative: “Let the thief no longer steal, but rather let him labor, doing honest work with his own hands, so that he may have something to share with anyone in need” (Ephesians 4:28). The cure for stealing is not only stopping but working and giving. The gospel turns a taker into a giver.

Agur prayed, “give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the food that is needful for me, lest I be full and deny you and say, ‘Who is the LORD?’ or lest I be poor and steal and profane the name of my God” (Proverbs 30:8–9). A contented heart is the best protection against stealing.

Robbing God

Malachi asked, “Will man rob God? Yet you are robbing me” (Malachi 3:8); the people had withheld their tithes and offerings. The eighth commandment assumes that people may rightly own property. Yet “the earth is the LORD’s and the fullness thereof” (Psalm 24:1). We are stewards, not absolute owners, called to use our resources for God’s glory and others’ good.

Making it right

In the Old Testament, thieves were required to repay, often several times over (Exodus 22:1). When Zacchaeus came to Christ he said, “And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold” (Luke 19:8). Repentance for theft includes making things right where possible.

Is there anything in your life — at work, at home or online — that amounts to stealing or unfaithfulness?

For reflection

How does Jesus deepen the seventh commandment? In what subtle ways might you be breaking the eighth? How does Ephesians 4:28 show its positive side? How can you guard your heart and eyes this week?

6.title: Truth, Contentment and the Law Fulfilled
6.essay:
The last two commandments guard truth and the heart. And then the whole law points us to the one who kept it.

You shall not bear false witness

“You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor” (Exodus 20:16). The commandment first concerned testimony in court, where lies could destroy a person. But it reaches all our speech: lying, slander, gossip, flattery and deception. It also calls us to speak the truth, to defend the reputation of others and to keep our promises. The Tongue study treats this more fully.

You shall not covet

“You shall not covet your neighbor’s house; you shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, or his male servant, or his female servant, or his ox, or his donkey, or anything that is your neighbor’s” (Exodus 20:17). The last commandment reaches into the heart. Coveting is an inner desire, invisible to others. It shows that God’s law is not only about actions but desires — that the whole law is ultimately about the heart.

Coveting is often the root of breaking the others. Ahab coveted Naboth’s vineyard. His wife Jezebel arranged false witnesses to accuse Naboth, who was stoned to death, and Ahab took the vineyard (1 Kings 21). Coveting led to false witness, murder and theft. The commandments stand or fall together.

The opposite of coveting is contentment: “be content with what you have, for he has said, ‘I will never leave you nor forsake you’” (Hebrews 13:5). Contentment rests on God’s presence, not our possessions.

Love fulfils the law

“Owe no one anything, except to love each other, for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law” (Romans 13:8). Paul gathers the second table — adultery, murder, stealing, coveting, “and any other commandment” — into one word: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” “Love does no wrong to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfilling of the law” (Romans 13:10). Love is not a replacement for the commandments. They are the shape love takes.

The law cannot save

No one is justified by keeping the law (Galatians 2:16). Every commandment, honestly examined, convicts us. That is one of its purposes: “So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith” (Galatians 3:24).

Written on the heart

God promised a new covenant, unlike the one Israel broke: “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they shall be my people” (Jeremiah 31:33). All would know him, and he would forgive their sin. What the stone tablets could not achieve, the Spirit accomplishes. The law that once condemned us now describes the life the Spirit is producing in us.

“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). The law could not save us because of the weakness of our flesh. So God, “by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, … condemned sin in the flesh, in order that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit” (Romans 8:3–4). The law’s goal is reached through the gospel, not by our own strength but by the Spirit’s work.

So once justified by faith, believers delight in God’s law as a guide for grateful living. “For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments. And his commandments are not burdensome” (1 John 5:3).

Christ, the law-keeper

Only one person has ever kept the Ten Commandments perfectly: Jesus Christ. He loved God with all his heart and his neighbour as himself. His perfect obedience is credited to all who trust him, and by his Spirit he is making them like himself.

A Christian reads through the Ten Commandments slowly, asking how he has broken each one in thought, word and deed. By the end he is humbled, seeing that he has broken them all in his heart. Then he reads Romans 8:1. He has never been so grateful for the gospel, or so eager to obey.

Read through the commandments and ask how each applies to your heart. Then thank God for Christ, who kept them for you.

For reflection

How is coveting often the root of breaking the other commandments? Read Romans 13:8–10: how does love fulfil the law? What does it mean to have God’s law written on your heart? Which commandment convicts you most, and how does Christ’s perfect obedience answer it?
